title: The Cimmerians, people of the mist
greek: Κιμμερίων ἀνδρῶν δῆμός τε πόλις τε, / ἠέρι καὶ νεφέλῃ κεκαλυμμένοι (Kimmeriōn andrōn dēmos te polis te, ēeri kai nephelēi kekalymmenoi)
short: At the edge of the world, by Oceanus, lives a people the sun never looks upon: 'baneful night is spread over wretched mortals'.
body: Historical Cimmerians were a nomadic people from north of the Black Sea who invaded Asia Minor in the seventh century BC (Herodotus 4.11-12, 1.15). Merry and Riddell distinguish them from Homer's Cimmerians, who represent a land of darkness, and suggest that the description may reflect reports of the long dark winters of the far north. They also mention an ancient variant reading Cheimerioi, 'wintry people', of which the name might be a slightly altered form. Homer's sunless land is the counterpart of the Laestrygonians' almost nightless one (10.82-86) and lies at the boundary where the sun does not shine (Nagy). It is the threshold of the dead, not yet the underworld itself.

title: The Nekyia: the dead rise from Erebus
greek: αἱ δ᾽ ἀγέροντο / ψυχαὶ ὑπὲξ Ἐρέβευς νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων (hai d' ageronto psychai hypex Erebeus nekyōn katatethnēōtōn)
short: When the blood flows into the pit, the souls (psychai) gather out of Erebus: brides, young men, old men, maidens, and warriors still in bloody armour.
body: Book 11 was called in antiquity the Nekyia, from the Greek for a rite of raising the dead (nekyomanteia, consultation of the dead). Erebos is the darkness under the earth, the realm of the dead, already mentioned at 10.528. The list of the dead, from brides to fallen soldiers 'wearing their blood-stained armour', is a small catalogue of all human life cut short, and the 'wondrous cry' of the crowd brings 'pale fear' (chlōron deos). Scholars have long debated the structure of the book: Odysseus seems to stay by his pit and call the dead up, yet in the later part (from 11.565) he appears to see figures inside Hades. Many critics, ancient and modern, have thought that parts of the book were added later; others defend its unity as a deliberate movement from consultation to vision.

title: Elpenor's plea for burial
greek: μή μ᾽ ἄκλαυτον ἄθαπτον ἰὼν ὄπιθεν καταλείπειν ... μή τοί τι θεῶν μήνιμα γένωμαι (mē m' aklauton athapton iōn opithen kataleipein ... mē toi ti theōn mēnima genōmai)
short: The first ghost to arrive is the unburied Elpenor, who begs for cremation, a mound, and his oar planted on top, warning that neglect would bring the gods' anger.
body: In Greek belief the unburied dead could not enter Hades fully, and leaving a comrade 'unwept and unburied' was a serious offence against the gods. Elpenor threatens that he might become a mēnima, a cause of divine wrath (mēnis), against Odysseus. The scene closely recalls the ghost of Patroclus appearing to Akhilleus to demand burial (Il. 23.65-92). Elpenor asks for the full rites: burning with his armour, a mound (sēma) 'on the shore of the grey sea' so that 'men yet to be may learn of me', and his oar fixed upon it. Nagy discusses the sēma and the oar, and connects them with Teiresias' prophecy of the oar mistaken for a winnowing fan. Virgil reworks the scene in Palinurus' plea (Aeneid 6.337-383).

anchor: Anticleia, the daughter of great-hearted Autolycus
title: Anticleia, daughter of Autolycus
greek: μητρὸς κατατεθνηυίης, / Αὐτολύκου θυγάτηρ μεγαλήτορος, Ἀντίκλεια (mētros katatethnēuiēs, Autolykou thygatēr megalētoros, Antikleia)
short: Odysseus' mother, alive when he left for Troy, appears among the dead; he must refuse her the blood until Teiresias has spoken.
body: Anticleia's father Autolycus ('the wolf himself') was the master thief and perjurer of Greek legend, who 'surpassed all men in thievery and oaths', a gift from Hermes (19.394-398); it was he who named the baby Odysseus (19.406-409). Odysseus' cunning thus has a pedigree. The scene of refusal is one of the most painful in the poem: Odysseus weeps and pities her, but holds his sword over the blood 'for all my great sorrow' (11.88-89). Ritual duty and the purpose of the journey come before personal feeling, as Teiresias must be consulted first. The reader learns of her death here for the first time, together with Odysseus; Eumaeus later tells how she died of grief (15.355-360).

title: Teiresias' prophecy and Thrinacia
greek: ὁππότε κε πρῶτον πελάσῃς εὐεργέα νῆα / Θρινακίῃ νήσῳ (oppote ke prōton pelasēis euergea nēa Thrinakiēi nēsōi)
short: Teiresias foretells Poseidon's anger, the test of the Sun's cattle on Thrinacia, a lonely late return on a foreign ship, and the suitors in his house.
body: The prophecy is an outline of the rest of the Odyssey. The decisive condition is Thrinacia: if the crew leave Helios' cattle unharmed, they may reach Ithaca 'though in evil plight'; if not, Odysseus will lose them all. Lines 11.114-115 repeat Polyphemus' curse almost word for word (9.534-535), showing that the curse will be fulfilled. Thrinacia was identified in antiquity with Sicily, called Trinakria, 'three-cornered' (Thucydides 6.2.2), and ancient readers took the name in that sense, though Homer gives no such hint. Teiresias carries a golden sceptre (11.91), a sign of authority; Nagy links it to the kingship Odysseus will regain. Note that Teiresias says nothing about Scylla, Charybdis or the Sirens: the practical directions come from Circe (12.37-141).

title: Helios, who sees all and hears all
greek: Ἠελίου, ὃς πάντ᾽ ἐφορᾷ καὶ πάντ᾽ ἐπακούει (Ēeliou, hos pant' ephorāi kai pant' epakouei)
short: The Sun, who travels over the whole world each day, is the all-seeing witness; for that reason the theft of his cattle cannot go unnoticed.
body: The same line is used in the Iliad when Agamemnon calls Helios to witness the oath before the duel of Paris and Menelaus (Il. 3.277), since a god who sees everything is the natural guarantor of oaths. In the Odyssey Helios is the informer who sees Ares and Aphrodite together and tells Hephaestus (8.270-271, 8.302). The formula is repeated by Odysseus on Thrinacia (12.323), and the irony is pointed: the all-seeing god learns of the slaughter of his cattle not by seeing it but from his daughter Lampetie (12.374-375). The archive's text prints 'over sees' here; the sense is 'oversees', as in the repetition at 12.323 ('oversees all things').

anchor: a winnowing-fan on thy stout shoulder
title: The oar mistaken for a winnowing fan
greek: ὁππότε κεν δή τοι ξυμβλήμενος ἄλλος ὁδίτης / φήῃ ἀθηρηλοιγὸν ἔχειν ἀνὰ φαιδίμῳ ὤμῳ (oppote ken dē toi xymblēmenos allos hoditēs phēēi athērēloigon echein ana phaidimōi ōmōi)
short: After killing the suitors, Odysseus must walk inland with an oar until someone calls it a winnowing fan; there he must plant it and sacrifice to Poseidon.
body: Athērēloigos, 'chaff-destroyer', is a winnowing shovel, used to toss threshed grain into the wind so that the chaff blows away; in shape it resembles an oar. The sign marks the place where the sea-god's power ends: there Odysseus will found, in effect, a cult of Poseidon among people who never knew him. The prescribed sacrifice of a ram, a bull and a boar (a triple offering, later called trittys) is unusual and solemn. Odysseus repeats the prophecy to Penelope (23.264-284), so it frames the end of the poem. Nagy reads the planted oar as a sēma, a sign with two meanings like Elpenor's oar on his tomb (12.15): 'the seafarer is dead' and 'the harvest is done', and connects it with cult of Odysseus as a hero.

title: Death 'far from the sea' or 'out of the sea'?
greek: θάνατος δέ τοι ἐξ ἁλὸς αὐτῷ / ἀβληχρὸς μάλα τοῖος ἐλεύσεται (thanatos de toi ex halos autōi ablēchros mala toios eleusetai)
short: Teiresias foretells a gentle death in sleek old age among a prosperous people; but ex halos can mean 'away from the sea' or 'from out of the sea'.
body: Murray, like most translators, takes ex halos as 'far from the sea', which suits the inland journey. But the Greek can equally mean 'out of the sea', and that reading fits a later epic, the Telegony (ascribed to Eugammon of Cyrene), in which Odysseus is killed by Telegonus, his son by Circe, with a spear tipped with the spine of a sting-ray. Merry and Riddell set out the arguments, observing that ablēchros in Homer means 'feeble' rather than 'gentle', and they suspect that the passage was shaped by, or added under the influence of, the later legend. Nagy reads the closing words, 'thy people shall dwell in prosperity (olbioi) around thee', as hinting at a hero-cult. The ambiguity may be deliberate: oracles are famously double.

title: Anticleia's death from longing
greek: ἀλλά με σός τε πόθος σά τε μήδεα, φαίδιμ᾽ Ὀδυσσεῦ, / σή τ᾽ ἀγανοφροσύνη μελιηδέα θυμὸν ἀπηύρα (alla me sos te pothos sa te mēdea, phaidim' Odysseu, sē t' aganophrosynē meliēdea thymon apēura)
short: Anticleia reports on Ithaca: Penelope waiting, Telemachus in charge, Laertes sleeping in the ashes, and herself dead of longing for her son's counsels and kindness.
body: The speech answers Odysseus' questions in reverse order and is one of the poem's most moving passages. Penelope 'abides with steadfast heart'; Telemachus holds the estate, a statement that does not quite fit the situation of Books 1-4, perhaps because Anticleia speaks of an earlier time; Laertes lives on his farm, sleeping among the slaves by the fire in winter and on fallen leaves in summer, a picture that prepares Book 24. The climax uses a tricolon, 'longing for you, your counsels (mēdea), your gentleness (aganophrosynē)', which echoes the 'gentle shafts' (aganois beleessin) of Odysseus' question: a sudden painless death, which Homer attributes to the arrows of Artemis for women and of Apollo for men (compare 15.409-411). Pothos, desire for the absent, is the emotion that runs through the Odyssey's family relations.

title: The threefold embrace
greek: τρὶς μὲν ἐφωρμήθην, ἑλέειν τέ με θυμὸς ἀνώγει, / τρὶς δέ μοι ἐκ χειρῶν σκιῇ εἴκελον ἢ καὶ ὀνείρῳ / ἔπτατ᾽ (tris men ephōrmēthēn, heleein te me thymos anōgei, tris de moi ek cheirōn skiēi eikelon ē kai oneirōi eptat')
short: Three times Odysseus tries to hold his mother, and three times she slips through his arms 'like a shadow or a dream'.
body: The scene has a close Iliadic model: Akhilleus reaches out to embrace the ghost of Patroclus, which vanishes 'like smoke' (Il. 23.99-101). The triple attempt is a typical pattern of failure in Homer. Virgil imitated these lines twice, in Aeneas' attempt to embrace the ghost of Creusa (Aeneid 2.792-794) and of his father Anchises (Aeneid 6.700-702), with almost identical wording: 'ter conatus ibi collo dare bracchia circum'. Dante echoes them in Purgatorio 2, where he fails to embrace his friend Casella. Odysseus' immediate fear that this is a phantom (eidōlon) sent by Persephone to deceive him leads to his mother's explanation of what death is.

title: What death is: the psyche like a dream
greek: ψυχὴ δ᾽ ἠΰτ᾽ ὄνειρος ἀποπταμένη πεπότηται (psychē d' ēyt' oneiros apoptamenē pepotētai)
short: Anticleia explains: at death fire destroys flesh and bones, and the psyche flies off like a dream and hovers about.
body: This is Homer's fullest statement of what happens at death. The 'appointed way' (dikē) of mortals is that the sinews no longer bind flesh and bones, which the fire consumes after cremation, while the psychē, the breath-soul that leaves the body at death, departs 'like a dream'. The psychē in Homer is not the seat of thought or feeling during life (those are thymos, phrenes, nóos), but a shadowy double that survives without strength or mind. Nagy comments on the comparison with a dream as implying unconsciousness. Anticleia ends by urging her son to hurry back to the light and remember all this to tell his wife, a gesture that makes Penelope the future audience of the story.

anchor: wives and the daughters of chieftains
title: The Catalogue of Heroines
greek: ὅσσαι ἀριστήων ἄλοχοι ἔσαν ἠδὲ θύγατρες (hossai aristēōn alochoi esan ēde thygatres)
short: Persephone sends up the wives and daughters of heroes, and Odysseus lets them drink one by one: a catalogue of famous women and their children.
body: The catalogue lists fourteen women, mostly mothers of heroic families, often by a god: Tyro, Antiope, Alcmene, Megara, Epicaste, Chloris, Leda, Iphimedeia, Phaedra, Procris, Ariadne, Maera, Clymene and Eriphyle. It belongs to a genre represented by the Hesiodic Catalogue of Women (Ehoiai), a lost poem of genealogies that began each entry 'or such as...'. The choice of material is often thought to suit the audience, since it is addressed to a court dominated by a queen, Arete, who speaks first when Odysseus pauses (11.336-341). Nagy declines to comment at length and refers to the analysis by Douglas Frame (2009). Several entries connect with the poem's themes of marriage and fidelity: Epicaste's incest, Eriphyle's betrayal of her husband.

title: Tyro and Poseidon
greek: Τυρὼ ... ἣ φάτο Σαλμωνῆος ἀμύμονος ἔκγονος εἶναι (Tyrō ... hē phato Salmōnēos amymonos ekgonos einai)
short: Tyro loved the river Enipeus; Poseidon took the river's shape and fathered Pelias and Neleus, founders of the royal lines of Iolcus and Pylos.
body: The first and fullest entry in the catalogue. Tyro is the daughter of Salmoneus and wife of Cretheus, son of Aeolus (not the Aeolus of Book 10). The union with Poseidon, disguised as the river she loved, is told with striking images: a dark wave 'stood about them like a mountain, vaulted-over' and hid them. The god's words after the union follow a typical pattern: a promise of glorious children and an instruction to keep silent. Her sons link the catalogue to the heroic world of the poem: Neleus is Nestor's father (11.281-286), and Pelias is the king who sent Jason for the Golden Fleece (Jason's father Aeson is her son by Cretheus). Sophocles wrote two plays named Tyro, now lost.

title: Epicaste (Jocasta) and Oedipus
greek: μητέρα τ᾽ Οἰδιπόδαο ἴδον, καλὴν Ἐπικάστην (mētera t' Oidipodao idon, kalēn Epikastēn)
short: Homer's version of the Oedipus story: the mother marries her son in ignorance, hangs herself, and Oedipus goes on ruling Thebes amid suffering.
body: Epicaste is the name Homer uses for the woman later called Jocasta. The essentials of the myth are already here: parricide, incest 'in ignorance of mind', and suicide by hanging. But there are notable differences from Sophocles' Oedipus the King: the gods made the truth known 'straightway' (anapysta, 11.274), and Oedipus does not blind himself or go into exile but continues as king, 'suffering woes'. The Iliad mentions funeral games for Oedipus at Thebes (Il. 23.679-680), so he died there as king. The 'Avengers of a mother' are the Erinyes (Furies), who punish crimes against kin; here they pursue Oedipus on his mother's behalf.

title: Eriphyle, who sold her husband for gold
greek: στυγερήν τ᾽ Ἐριφύλην, / ἣ χρυσὸν φίλου ἀνδρὸς ἐδέξατο τιμήεντα (stygerēn t' Eriphylēn, hē chryson philou andros edexato timēenta)
short: The last named woman of the catalogue: bribed with a golden necklace, Eriphyle persuaded her husband Amphiaraus to join the fatal expedition against Thebes.
body: Amphiaraus, a seer, knew that he would die if he joined the Seven against Thebes, but he had agreed that his wife would settle disputes between him and Adrastus. Polynices bribed her with the necklace of Harmonia, and she sent him to his death (Apollodorus 3.6.2). The Odyssey alludes to the story again when it says that Amphiaraus died at Thebes 'because of a woman's gifts' (gynaiōn heineka dōrōn, 15.247), the same phrase used later in this book of Eurypylus' death (11.521), as Merry and Riddell note. Eriphyle is one of a series of faithless wives (Clytemnestra, Helen) set against Penelope, and the catalogue thus ends on the theme that Agamemnon's ghost will develop.

anchor: held spell-bound throughout the shadowy halls
title: The Intermezzo: the spell of the story
greek: ὣς ἔφαθ᾽, οἱ δ᾽ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ, / κηληθμῷ δ᾽ ἔσχοντο κατὰ μέγαρα σκιόεντα (hōs ephath', hoi d' ara pantes akēn egenonto siōpēi, kēlēthmōi d' eschonto kata megara skioenta)
short: Odysseus breaks off his tale; the Phaeacians sit 'spell-bound' (kēlēthmos), Arete calls for more gifts, and Alcinous begs him to continue through the night.
body: This interruption in the middle of the Apologoi (often called the Intermezzo) returns us to the frame of the story in Scheria. Kēlēthmos, 'enchantment', is the spell of song, related to kēleō, 'charm'; the same lines describe the Phaeacians' response at the end of the tale (13.1-2). Arete, whose favour Nausicaa and Athena said was decisive (6.310-315, 7.53-77), now claims Odysseus as 'my guest' and urges generosity. The pause is also a negotiation: Odysseus says he would gladly stay a year for more gifts (11.355-361). Nagy argues that it shows the performance is not over-long, and that the second half of the Nekyia, with the heroes of Troy, is presented as a special request by the audience.

title: Odysseus as a bard: truth and lies
greek: μῦθον δ᾽ ὡς ὅτ᾽ ἀοιδὸς ἐπισταμένως κατέλεξας (mython d' hōs hot' aoidos epistamenōs katelexas)
short: Alcinous assures Odysseus that he is no cheat or liar: his words have 'grace' (morphē) and he has told his tale with skill, like a professional singer.
body: Alcinous contrasts Odysseus with the many vagabonds 'that fashion lies out of what no man can even see' (11.364-366). The compliment is double-edged for the reader: Odysseus is the great liar of the poem, who will tell long false tales about himself in Ithaca (13.256-286, 14.192-359, 19.165-202), and here he holds his audience with stories that no one else can confirm. The comparison with the aoidos (singer) makes Odysseus a figure of the epic poet himself; in Book 21 he will string his bow as a singer strings a lyre (21.406-409). Later critics, from Juvenal (15.13-26), who calls him a liar telling tall tales to the Phaeacians, to modern narratologists, have explored the unreliability of the Apologoi.

anchor: slays an ox at the stall
title: Agamemnon's death: an ox at the manger, swine at a feast
greek: ἔκτα σὺν οὐλομένῃ ἀλόχῳ, οἶκόνδε καλέσσας, / δειπνίσσας, ὥς τίς τε κατέκτανε βοῦν ἐπὶ φάτνῃ (ekta syn oulomenēi alochōi, oikonde kalessas, deipnissas, hōs tis te katektane boun epi phatnēi)
short: Agamemnon tells how Aegisthus and Clytemnestra killed him at a feast 'as one slays an ox at the stall', his men butchered like swine for a banquet.
body: The story of Agamemnon's homecoming is the Odyssey's constant counter-example, told by Zeus (1.35-43), Nestor (3.254-312) and Menelaus (4.512-537); here the victim tells it himself, with the bitterest details. The similes are sacrificial: the king dies like a feeding ox, his comrades like white-tusked swine slaughtered for a wedding or a club dinner (eranos). The feast, the sacred act of hospitality, becomes the occasion of murder, a perversion of xenia like the Cyclops' meal. Cassandra, Priam's daughter and Agamemnon's captive, is killed beside him; Clytemnestra does not even close his eyes and mouth, the most basic rite for the dead. Aeschylus' Agamemnon (458 BC) relocates the murder to the bath.

title: Agamemnon's advice: Penelope and Clytemnestra
greek: οὐκέτι πιστὰ γυναιξίν (ouketi pista gynaixin)
short: Agamemnon warns Odysseus to land secretly and trust no woman, while admitting that the 'very prudent' Penelope will not kill him.
body: The speech is contradictory in a revealing way. Agamemnon praises Penelope, 'wise Penelope, daughter of Icarius', as unlike Clytemnestra, and then concludes that 'no longer is there faith in women'. The advice to land secretly is exactly what Odysseus will do in Book 13, with Athena's help, and his testing of Penelope before revealing himself follows the spirit of the warning. The contrast between Clytemnestra and Penelope is completed in Book 24, where Agamemnon's ghost praises Penelope's kleos and contrasts it with Clytemnestra's 'hateful song' (24.192-202). Nagy notes that in 11.433 Clytemnestra's deed is said to bring shame on all women, even the good. Agamemnon's question about Orestes ironically echoes Odysseus' own uncertainty about his son.

title: Akhilleus: better a hired labourer alive than king of the dead
greek: βουλοίμην κ᾽ ἐπάρουρος ἐὼν θητευέμεν ἄλλῳ, / ἀνδρὶ παρ᾽ ἀκλήρῳ, ᾧ μὴ βίοτος πολὺς εἴη, / ἢ πᾶσιν νεκύεσσι καταφθιμένοισιν ἀνάσσειν (bouloimēn k' eparouros eōn thēteuemen allōi, andri par' aklērōi, hōi mē biotos polys eiē, ē pasin nekyessi kataphthimenoisin anassein)
short: Akhilleus rejects Odysseus' consolation: he would rather be a landless man's hired hand on earth than rule all the dead.
body: A thēs was a free labourer working for hire, lower in security than a slave attached to a household; eparouros means 'bound to the soil', and Merry and Riddell compare the medieval serf. The master is himself aklēros, without an allotment of land. The speech seems to reverse the choice Akhilleus made in the Iliad, where he accepted a short life with undying kleos rather than a long life without glory (Il. 9.410-416). Critics debate whether it is a recantation, a statement about death that does not cancel the value of kleos, or a sign of the Odyssey's preference for survival over heroic death. Plato's Socrates wanted these lines struck out of poetry, as making death seem terrible to future soldiers (Republic 3.386c). Akhilleus is comforted only by news of his son's valour (11.538-540).

title: 'The unheeding dead, the phantoms of men outworn'
greek: ἔνθα τε νεκροὶ / ἀφραδέες ναίουσι, βροτῶν εἴδωλα καμόντων (entha te nekroi aphradees naiousi, brotōn eidōla kamontōn)
short: Akhilleus describes Hades as the home of the senseless dead, mere images (eidōla) of mortals who are 'worn out'.
body: Aphradēs means 'without understanding, senseless': in Hades the dead lack the faculties that made them persons. Kamontes ('those who have toiled, are worn out') is a euphemism for the dead. Eidōlon, 'image', is the word for the phantom that resembles a living person; Odysseus feared that his mother was an eidōlon sent by Persephone (11.213), and Heracles in Hades is only his eidōlon (11.602). Nagy comments that the dead are non-conscious because they are in Hades. The view is consistent with Circe's statement that only Teiresias keeps his wits (10.494-495), and it explains why the shades must drink blood before they can recognise and speak.

title: Neoptolemus and the Wooden Horse
greek: ἵππον, ὃν κάμ᾽ Ἐπειός (hippon, hon kam' Epeios)
short: Odysseus comforts Akhilleus with the deeds of his son Neoptolemus: brilliant in council and battle, and fearless inside the Wooden Horse.
body: Neoptolemus, brought from Scyros by Odysseus himself, appears in the Iliad only in passing (Il. 19.326-327); his deeds belonged to the later epics of the Trojan cycle, the Little Iliad and the Sack of Troy. Odysseus' account of the Horse complements Demodocus' song (8.499-520) and Menelaus' story (4.271-289): the other leaders weep and tremble, while the young man grips his sword and begs to be let out. Epeus, the builder of the Horse, is the boxer of the funeral games in Iliad 23. The picture is selective: Odysseus says nothing of the later tradition that Neoptolemus killed Priam at the altar (as in Virgil, Aeneid 2.526-558) and hurled Astyanax from the walls (as in the lost Little Iliad). Akhilleus departs 'with long strides over the field of asphodel', joyful at his son's fame.

title: Eurypylus son of Telephus and the Ceteians
greek: Τηλεφίδην ... ἥρω᾽ Εὐρύπυλον, πολλοὶ δ᾽ ἀμφ᾽ αὐτὸν ἑταῖροι / Κήτειοι κτείνοντο γυναίων εἵνεκα δώρων (Tēlephidēn ... hērō' Eurypylon, polloi d' amph' auton hetairoi Kēteioi kteinonto gynaiōn heineka dōrōn)
short: Neoptolemus' great victim was Eurypylus, a Mysian ally of Troy, who came with his people the Ceteians 'because of gifts a woman craved'.
body: Eurypylus, son of Telephus king of Mysia, was the last great ally to come to Troy, in the Little Iliad. The 'gifts' refer to a story preserved by ancient commentators: his mother Astyoche, Priam's sister, was bribed with a golden vine to send her son to the war, a close parallel to Eriphyle (15.247). The Ceteians puzzled ancient scholars: Merry and Riddell quote Strabo's complaint (Geography 13, p. 615 Casaubon) that no one knows who they were, and record the modern suggestion, now widely discussed, that the name preserves the Hittites (Hatti, Kheta), the great Anatolian power of the Late Bronze Age. Odysseus also mentions Memnon, the Ethiopian prince killed by Akhilleus in the Aethiopis, as the only man handsomer than Eurypylus.

title: The meadow of asphodel
greek: κατ᾽ ἀσφοδελὸν λειμῶνα (kat' asphodelon leimōna)
short: The dead walk in a meadow of asphodel, a pale-flowered plant of the lily family, food of the poor and planted on graves.
body: Asphodel (Asphodelus) is a tall plant with grey-green leaves and white or pale pink star-shaped flowers, common on Greek hillsides. Merry and Riddell explain its association with the dead from ancient custom: Pliny reports that its root was eaten by the poor and placed on tombs, and Hesiod names it with mallow as the humble food of the frugal (Works and Days 41). They also note that it was planted on graves in their own day, perhaps to give the dead a simple meal. The phrase recurs at 11.573 (Orion hunting) and 24.13, where the suitors' souls are led down. Later poets turned the meadow into the Elysian 'asphodel' of English poetry (Pope, Tennyson).

anchor: he answered me not a word
title: The silence of Aias
greek: ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δέ μ᾽ οὐδὲν ἀμείβετο, βῆ δὲ μετ᾽ ἄλλας / ψυχὰς εἰς Ἔρεβος νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων (hōs ephamēn, ho de m' ouden ameibeto, bē de met' allas psychas eis Erebos nekyōn katatethnēōtōn)
short: Aias, still angry over losing Akhilleus' arms to Odysseus, refuses to answer his conciliatory speech and walks away into Erebus.
body: After Akhilleus' death his armour was offered as a prize for the best of the Greeks; the judges, Odysseus says, were 'the sons of the Trojans and Pallas Athena', and Odysseus won. Aias, humiliated, killed himself, as told in the lost Little Iliad and in Sophocles' Ajax. Odysseus' speech is generous: he wishes he had never won, calls Aias 'a tower of strength' (pyrgos), and blames Zeus. Aias' silence is the most eloquent answer in the book. The author of On the Sublime (9.2) cites it as an example of greatness of mind expressed without words, 'nobler than any speech'. Virgil imitates the scene when Dido turns away from Aeneas in silence in the underworld (Aeneid 6.469-473). Nagy notes that Aias, not Odysseus, is called second best to Akhilleus (11.550-551).

anchor: Minos, the glorious son of Zeus
title: Minos the judge and the 'Great Sinners'
greek: ἔνθ᾽ ἦ τοι Μίνωα ἴδον, Διὸς ἀγλαὸν υἱόν, / χρύσεον σκῆπτρον ἔχοντα, θεμιστεύοντα νέκυσσιν (enth' ē toi Minōa idon, Dios aglaon huion, chryseon skēptron echonta, themisteuonta nekyssin)
short: Odysseus now seems to see inside Hades: Minos, king of Crete, giving judgments among the dead, followed by Orion and the punished sinners.
body: Minos, son of Zeus and Europa, ruled Crete (19.178-179). Here he gives themistes, 'judgments', to the dead who ask him for them: he continues among the shades the activity of a king in life, rather than judging souls for their deeds on earth. Plato later made him, with Rhadamanthys and Aeacus, a judge of the dead who sends souls to reward or punishment (Gorgias 523e-524a). From this point to 11.627 the narrative changes: Odysseus no longer waits at the pit for the dead to come, but describes figures doing things in Hades. The narrative could pass directly from 11.565 to 11.630, and many critics since antiquity (Merry and Riddell discuss the question) have thought the whole passage (the 'Great Sinners' or 'Hades vision') a later addition; others defend it as an original climax.

title: Tityos and the vultures
greek: καὶ Τιτυὸν εἶδον, Γαίης ἐρικυδέος υἱόν (kai Tityon eidon, Gaiēs erikydeos huion)
short: The giant Tityos lies stretched over nine plethra while two vultures tear his liver, punishment for assaulting Leto on her way to Pytho (Delphi).
body: Tityos is the first of three great sinners whose punishments are described. Each is eternal and repetitive, and each crime is an offence against the gods. Tityos assaulted Leto, mother of Apollo and Artemis, as she travelled to Pytho (the old name of Delphi) through Panopeus in Phocis. The liver, seat of desire in Greek thought, is the organ punished; compare Prometheus' liver eaten by an eagle (Hesiod, Theogony 523-525). A plethron was about 30 metres, so his body covers an enormous area. The Phaeacians' ships once took Rhadamanthys to visit Tityos in Euboea (7.321-324). Polygnotus painted Tityos, Tantalus and Sisyphus in his famous Underworld painting at Delphi, described by Pausanias (10.28-31).

title: Tantalus
greek: καὶ μὴν Τάνταλον εἰσεῖδον κρατέρ᾽ ἄλγε᾽ ἔχοντα (kai mēn Tantalon eiseidon krater' alge' echonta)
short: Standing in water to his chin under fruit-laden trees, Tantalus can never drink or eat: water and branches withdraw whenever he reaches for them.
body: The punishment gives English the verb 'tantalize'. Homer does not state the crime. Later sources give several: Pindar says that he stole the gods' nectar and ambrosia to give to mortals, rejecting the story that he served his son Pelops to the gods at a feast (Olympian 1.36-64); others say he revealed the gods' secrets. Pindar also knows a different punishment, a stone hanging over his head (Olympian 1.57-58). The description is built with careful parallelism: 'as often as that old man stooped down... so often would the water be swallowed up', and the same 'as often as' for the fruit. Plato's Socrates lists Tantalus, Sisyphus and Tityos, citing Homer, as the type of incurable sinners punished in Hades (Gorgias 525e).

sources.cite: Homer, Odyssey 11.582-592 (Greek text, ed. A. T. Murray, Loeb, 1919)

title: Sisyphus and the 'ruthless stone'
greek: αὖτις ἔπειτα πέδονδε κυλίνδετο λᾶας ἀναιδής (autis epeita pedonde kylindeto lāas anaidēs)
short: Sisyphus endlessly rolls a huge stone up a hill; just before the top it rolls back, 'shameless', to the plain.
body: Sisyphus, king of Ephyra (Corinth), is called 'craftiest of men' in the Iliad (Il. 6.153); later stories told of his tricks on the gods and on Death itself, and some made him the real father of Odysseus. The stone is anaidēs, 'without shame or respect', a personification which Murray renders 'ruthless'. Aristotle cites this line as an example of the vivid style that gives life and activity to inanimate things (Rhetoric 3.11.3, 1411b33-1412a). The sound of the Greek, heavy and slow as he pushes upward and rushing in dactyls as the stone falls, was admired by Dionysius of Halicarnassus (On Literary Composition 20). Nagy comments on krataiis, 'the Force', in the previous line (11.597), which he connects with the name of Scylla's mother Crataiis (12.124). Albert Camus made Sisyphus an emblem of absurd human labour (1942).

title: Heracles' phantom
greek: τὸν δὲ μετ᾽ εἰσενόησα βίην Ἡρακληείην, / εἴδωλον· αὐτὸς δὲ μετ᾽ ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι / τέρπεται ἐν θαλίῃς καὶ ἔχει καλλίσφυρον Ἥβην (ton de met' eisenoēsa biēn Hēraklēeiēn, eidōlon; autos de met' athanatoisi theoisi terpetai en thaliēis kai echei kallisphyron Hēbēn)
short: Odysseus sees only an 'image' of Heracles, since the hero himself is a god on Olympus married to Hebe; the lines that say so were suspected in antiquity.
body: The passage tries to reconcile two traditions: Heracles as a dead hero in Hades (as in Il. 18.117-119, where 'not even mighty Heracles escaped death') and Heracles deified and married to Hebe, daughter of Zeus and Hera. The solution, splitting the man into an eidōlon below and his 'self' (autos) above, is unique in Homer. Ancient critics found 11.602-604 suspect, and the scholia attribute them to Onomacritus, a sixth-century Athenian editor of oracles; Merry and Riddell think the rest of the Heracles scene genuine but those three lines a later insertion. The ghost's speech recalls his labours for Eurystheus, 'a man far worse than I', and his descent, guided by Hermes and Athena, to fetch 'the hound of Hades', the dog Hesiod first names Cerberus (Theogony 311): a hero who also suffered and also returned from the dead, a natural model for Odysseus. His gold baldric, decorated with beasts, battles and killings (11.609-614), is a small ecphrasis that recalls Akhilleus' shield.

title: The Gorgon's head
greek: μή μοι Γοργείην κεφαλὴν δεινοῖο πελώρου / ἐξ Ἄϊδος πέμψειεν ἀγαυὴ Περσεφόνεια (mē moi Gorgeiēn kephalēn deinoio pelōrou ex Aïdos pempseien agauē Persephoneia)
short: Odysseus flees in 'pale fear' that Persephone will send up the Gorgon's head, the petrifying face of terror itself.
body: In Homer the Gorgon is above all a face: the Gorgon's head appears on Athena's aegis (Il. 5.741-742) and on Agamemnon's shield (Il. 11.36-37), and Hector's glaring eyes are compared to the Gorgon's (Il. 8.349). Hesiod first tells of Medusa, beheaded by Perseus (Theogony 274-281); the power of her head to turn onlookers to stone appears in later poets (Pindar, Pythian 10.46-48). Here the Gorgon seems to be imagined as a guardian of the underworld, a terror that would end the encounter with death in death. The fear is decisive: Odysseus hurries back to his ship and down the stream of Oceanus. The ending mirrors the beginning of the book (11.43, 'pale fear seized me'), a ring composition that closes the Nekyia.
